problem: VLA models had not been applied to underwater robotics: end-to-end VLAs lack a hierarchy that fits bandwidth-limited acoustic links, need large amounts of expensive demonstration data, and have no real-time hydrodynamic compensation.
motivation: AUVs face nonlinear hydrodynamics, turbid and low-light sensing, and very limited communication, so conventional PID, RL and end-to-end policies are task-specific or data-hungry. Pretrained multimodal foundation models combined with physics priors could give a zero-underwater-data route to language-driven autonomy.
key_idea: A dual-brain VLA: a cloud VLM (QVQ-Max) decomposes the mission into CoT sub-goals during surfacing, an onboard Qwen2.5-VL-7B 'cerebellum' outputs discrete JSON actions, and a hydrodynamics-informed MPC executes them without training.
insight: Separating strategic planning from reactive execution lets the local model judge sub-task completion from its own visual feedback and skip redundant steps under turbidity. In the qualitative degraded-visibility test, the single-brain model kept going 'forward' after losing the target and overshot. The evidence is thin: a few real trials, one qualitative DBM-vs-SBM comparison, and no ablation of the MPC or CoT.
method: Dual-brain architecture: a cloud brain (QVQ-Max) runs intermittently during surfacing to produce long-horizon sub-goals, and an onboard Qwen(2.5)-VL-7B cerebellum runs closed-loop step-wise control.

CoT prompt framework: both brains output structured reasoning; the cerebellum emits a JSON tuple with reasoning, decision (forward/backward/left/right), velocity level (low/medium/high), sub_task_done and mission_done.
Discrete motion profiles: each command runs as a fixed 1 s trapezoidal profile, with translational speeds of 0.2/0.5/0.8 m/s and turn rates of 0.5/1.0/1.5 rad/s.

Hydrodynamics-informed MPC: the cost combines tracking error, thrust effort and quadratic drag (D_v v|v|, D_r r|r|), solved at a 0.02 s control interval, with thrust allocated through the pseudo-inverse B† and active braking at the end.

Online drag estimation: drag coefficients are estimated from IMU acceleration, thrust and added-mass-corrected mass/inertia, and phase-specific hydrodynamics are handled for the acceleration, constant-speed and deceleration phases.
Zero-data training: pretrained foundation models with prompt engineering and physics-based control, with no underwater demonstrations.

setting.backbone: QVQ-Max (cloud, frozen) + Qwen2.5-VL-7B (onboard, frozen) + physics-based MPC
setting.training_data: none (zero-data; prompts and physics-based MPC only)
setting.observation: monocular RGB camera images plus IMU
setting.action_space: discrete direction (forward/backward/left/right) with 3 velocity levels, executed as 1 s MPC motion primitives

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is used. The only quantitative results are small real-tank trials on custom tasks (Distinguish Letter 51/60, Go to Object 4/5, Go through Tunnel 4/5, Go to Object and avoid obstacle 3/5), compared against QUAR-VLA's simulation percentages. This is not a like-for-like comparison, and the DBM vs SBM comparison is qualitative only.
results: In real-tank trials the method reaches 51/60 on letter distinguishing, 4/5 on go-to-object, 4/5 on tunnel traversal and 3/5 on obstacle avoidance. The paper reports gains of +19% to +27% over QUAR-VLA's simulated baseline (66/60/53/41%) with 0 training data versus 262K. Under low light and high turbidity, the dual-brain model completes the task while the single-brain model overshoots.
limitations: The comparison is not like-for-like (real trials versus a simulated quadruped baseline from another paper), and the trial counts are tiny (5 per task).
There are no ablations of MPC, CoT or the dual-brain design, and the DBM vs SBM comparison is qualitative only.
Experiments were done in a lab tank with simulated turbidity, not the open ocean, and the discrete action space is coarse.
